note:
Telehealth visit by real-time video. The patient joined from his home on a tablet, audio and video quality were good, he was alone, and he gave verbal consent for a video visit. Reason for visit is follow-up of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in a 66-year-old male who takes an anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation.

Interval history: Over the last two months he reports a weaker urinary stream, hesitancy at the start of voiding, and a sense of incomplete emptying. He has nocturia three times per night and urgency during the day. He denies dysuria, gross hematuria, fever, flank pain, and back pain. He has never been unable to void. His primary care physician started oxybutynin 5 mg BID about a month ago for the urgency, and since then the hesitancy has gotten worse and he has dry mouth and constipation. He denies dizziness when he stands up. His symptom score (IPSS) completed during the call was 19, with a bother score of 4.

Past history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension (HTN), type 2 diabetes (T2DM), and hyperlipidemia. He read his pill bottles to me on camera. He first said his apixaban was 2.5 mg BID, and then he turned the bottle and corrected himself: the label reads 5 mg BID, which is the dose he has been taking without missed doses. His other medications are tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements this morning with his own cuff and scale were BP 134/80, HR 68, weight 92 kg, and fingerstick glucose 118 mg/dL. On video he looks comfortable and in no distress, speaks in full sentences, and walks steadily when asked to cross the room. An abdominal, genital, and rectal exam cannot be done by video, so suprapubic fullness and prostate size were not assessed today.

Results reviewed from last week: PSA 2.9 ng/mL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, eGFR 78, A1c 6.9%, and a urinalysis negative for blood, nitrite, and leukocyte esterase. At his in-person visit six weeks ago a bladder scan showed a post-void residual of 90 mL and a prostate ultrasound estimated the gland at 52 mL.

Impression: BPH with worsening LUTS, with oxybutynin likely contributing to the hesitancy. He is on apixaban for atrial fibrillation, so bleeding risk and any future procedure have to account for that.

Plan discussed with the patient using teach-back. Stop oxybutynin today. Increase tamsulosin from 0.4 mg to 0.8 mg daily, and check his BP sitting and standing at home for the first week and call if he feels lightheaded. Start finasteride 5 mg daily because the prostate is larger than 40 mL; I explained that it takes several months to work and will lower his PSA by about half, so today's 2.9 is the baseline. Continue apixaban 5 mg BID without interruption and avoid NSAIDs. Continue amlodipine, metformin, and atorvastatin as prescribed by primary care. Order a repeat urinalysis, uroflowmetry, and a repeat bladder scan at an in-person visit in six weeks. If medical therapy fails, surgical options such as TURP would be discussed, and any apixaban hold would be coordinated with cardiology. He was advised to go to the ED for gross hematuria, inability to void, or fever. Follow-up by video in six weeks.
summary: A 66-year-old male with benign prostatic hyperplasia and lower urinary tract symptoms, who takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation, was seen by video for a weaker stream, hesitancy, incomplete emptying and nocturia, with the hesitancy worse since oxybutynin was started by primary care. He denies dysuria, gross hematuria, fever and flank pain. Home BP was 134/80, PSA was 2.9 ng/mL, post-void residual was 90 mL and the prostate measured 52 mL. The impression is BPH with worsening symptoms to which oxybutynin is likely contributing. Oxybutynin is stopped, tamsulosin is increased to 0.8 mg daily, finasteride 5 mg daily is started, apixaban 5 mg BID continues, and uroflowmetry with a repeat bladder scan is planned in six weeks.

note:
Hospital day 3 for this 39-year-old female admitted with left-sided renal colic, during which a CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast incidentally showed a 3.1 cm right adrenal mass along with a 4 mm left ureteral stone. Endocrinology is following for the adrenal incidentaloma work-up. The mass measures 8 Hounsfield units, is homogeneous with smooth margins, and has no calcification, which favors a benign lipid-rich adenoma.

Her flank pain is much better today and she is tolerating oral intake. On targeted review she denies headaches, palpitations, sweating spells, easy bruising, and muscle weakness. She has hypertension diagnosed four years ago, treated with lisinopril 10 mg daily, and she says her home readings have been running high. She also uses over-the-counter supplements: biotin 10 mg daily for hair thinning and a licorice root extract capsule every morning for digestion. She has no history of cancer.

Vitals this morning are temperature 36.9 Celsius, BP 148/92, HR 78, RR 16, and SpO2 98% on room air. She is comfortable, with no moon facies, no abdominal striae, and no muscle weakness on rising from a chair. Mild left costovertebral angle tenderness remains.

The work-up so far shows normal plasma free metanephrines, which makes pheochromocytoma unlikely. A 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test gave a cortisol of 1.2 mcg/dL, which excludes autonomous cortisol secretion. Potassium is 3.4 mmol/L and creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. An aldosterone to renin ratio was drawn but is unreliable, because she is taking lisinopril and licorice root, and biotin can also interfere with the immunoassays used for these hormones.

Impression is a right adrenal incidentaloma that is most likely a benign non-functioning adenoma pending aldosterone testing, hypertension with mild hypokalemia that may be partly related to licorice root, and a left ureteral stone with renal colic that is improving.

Recommendations: stop the licorice root extract and hold the biotin for at least 72 hours before repeat labs. Change lisinopril to amlodipine 5 mg daily now so that renin and aldosterone can be interpreted later. Repeat the aldosterone to renin ratio and potassium as an outpatient in two weeks. No further imaging is needed for the mass given its low attenuation and size under 4 cm. Continue ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours as needed for stone pain, and urology will follow the stone. She will follow up in endocrinology clinic in four weeks and was counseled to bring every supplement to each visit.

Plasma metanephrines are normal and a dexamethasone suppression test excludes autonomous cortisol secretion, while the aldosterone to renin ratio is unreliable on current medications. The impression is a likely benign non-functioning adenoma with hypertension and mild hypokalemia. Licorice root is stopped, biotin is held, lisinopril is changed to amlodipine 5 mg daily, and aldosterone testing is repeated in two weeks.

note:
Doctor: Good morning, thanks for coming in. Before we start, let me confirm: you are a 41-year-old female, six weeks out from your cesarean delivery, right?
Patient: Yes, that's right. Baby girl, and she's doing great.
Doctor: Wonderful. How have you been feeling yourself?
Patient: Tired, mostly. The baby is up every two or three hours and I'm breastfeeding, so it's a lot. But no big problems.
Doctor: Tell me about the incision.
Patient: It's a little sore when I bend over, but it isn't red and nothing is leaking.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No, none.
Doctor: And your bleeding?
Patient: It's light now, just some spotting. It was heavy the first couple of weeks.
Doctor: Any calf pain or calf swelling? Any chest pain or trouble breathing?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: How is your mood? A lot of women feel very low after delivery.
Patient: I get weepy sometimes, but I'm not down all the time. I try to sleep when the baby sleeps.
Doctor: You filled out the Edinburgh questionnaire in the waiting room and your score was 6, which is reassuring.
Patient: Okay, good.
Doctor: I see you had high blood pressure at the end of the pregnancy and went home on labetalol 100 mg twice a day. Are you still taking it?
Patient: Yes, twice a day. I check at home and it's usually around 115 over 75.
Doctor: Today it's 118 over 76 with a heart rate of 74. Your hemoglobin at discharge was 9.6, so we rechecked it this morning. It's 10.8, still a bit low. Have you been taking any iron?
Patient: No, nobody told me to.
Doctor: Okay. I'll start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day. Take it with orange juice, not with your coffee, and it can make you constipated.
Patient: Alright. What about birth control? I definitely don't want another baby.
Doctor: Since you're breastfeeding, I'd avoid pills with estrogen. A levonorgestrel IUD is a great option, and I can place it at your next visit in two weeks. Until then, use condoms.
Patient: Okay, that works.
Doctor: On exam, your incision is clean, dry and well healed, your uterus is firm and back down in the pelvis, your lungs are clear, and your legs aren't swollen.
Doctor: So, you're recovering well from your cesarean delivery. Your blood pressure is normal now, so you can stop the labetalol. Keep checking at home for two more weeks and call me if it goes above 140 over 90. You have mild anemia, so start the iron, and we'll recheck your blood count in six weeks. Your mood screen is normal, but call us if the weepiness gets worse. Come back in two weeks for the IUD.
Patient: Thank you.
summary: A 41-year-old female, six weeks after a cesarean delivery and breastfeeding, attended her postpartum visit with fatigue, mild incision soreness and light spotting. She denies fever, chills, calf pain, calf swelling, chest pain and trouble breathing, and her Edinburgh score was 6. Blood pressure is 118/76 on labetalol, and hemoglobin has improved to 10.8 from 9.6. The impression is good recovery with normal blood pressure and mild anemia. Labetalol is stopped, ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day is started, a blood count is repeated in six weeks, and a levonorgestrel IUD is planned in two weeks.

Wants contraception and is breastfeeding.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 118 over 76, heart rate 74. Edinburgh questionnaire score 6. Hemoglobin 9.6 at discharge and 10.8 today. Incision clean, dry and well healed, uterus firm and back down in the pelvis, lungs clear, legs not swollen.
soap.assessment: Recovering well from cesarean delivery. Blood pressure now normal. Mild anemia. Mood screen normal.
plan: Stop labetalol
Continue home blood pressure checks for two more weeks and call if above 140 over 90
Start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day, taken with orange juice and not with coffee
Recheck blood count in six weeks
Place a levonorgestrel IUD at the next visit in two weeks, use condoms until then and avoid estrogen pills while breastfeeding
Call if the weepiness gets worse
Return in two weeks

note:
79-year-old male, ED return visit for R distal radius fx recheck. 1 wk s/p mechanical fall onto outstretched R hand (FOOSH) at home.
Initial ED visit 1 wk ago: closed reduction + sugar-tong splint, d/c'd home w/ ortho f/u.
Interval: wrist pain 4/10, improved on acetaminophen. Mild finger swelling, better w/ elevation. Denies numbness, tingling, or color change in fingers. No new falls. No HA, neck pain, or LOC at time of fall. No CP or palpitations before fall.
PMH: HTN, CKD stage 3, osteopenia on prior DEXA.
Social: lives w/ spouse, R-hand dominant, independent in ADLs at baseline, non-smoker.
Meds: amlodipine 5 mg daily. acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN. oxycodone 5 mg q6h PRN, used only 2 tabs total. No NSAIDs (CKD).
Vitals: BP 138/82, HR 76, RR 16, Temp 36.8 C, SpO2 97% RA.
Exam: splint intact, no skin breakdown or odor. Mild dorsal hand swelling. Fingers warm, cap refill <2 sec, sensation intact in median, ulnar, and radial distributions. Full finger ROM. Snuffbox NT. Elbow and shoulder NT.
Labs: Cr 1.4, eGFR 48.
XR R wrist 3 views in splint: extra-articular distal radius fx (Colles), dorsal angulation 8 deg, radial height 10 mm, alignment maintained vs post-reduction films. Ulnar styloid fx also noted.
Impression: R extra-articular distal radius fx, alignment maintained after closed reduction, nonop mgmt appropriate. Fragility fx w/ osteopenia.
Rec:
- Cont splint, elevation, finger ROM exercises
- D/c oxycodone. Change acetaminophen to 1000 mg q8h scheduled x 1 wk then PRN
- Start vit D3 2000 units daily + dietary calcium
- Ortho clinic in 1 wk w/ repeat XR, convert to short-arm cast
- Outpt DEXA + PCP f/u for osteoporosis tx
- Return precautions: worsening pain, numbness, cold or blue fingers, severe swelling
Pt verbalized understanding of plan and agrees.
summary: A 79-year-old male returned to the ED one week after a fall onto his outstretched right hand for recheck of a distal radius fracture treated with closed reduction and a sugar-tong splint. Pain is 4/10 and improving, and he denies numbness, tingling and color change in the fingers. Neurovascular exam is intact and the wrist film shows maintained alignment of an extra-articular fracture. The impression is a right extra-articular distal radius fracture suitable for nonoperative management, with a fragility fracture and osteopenia. Oxycodone is stopped, acetaminophen is scheduled, vitamin D3 is started, and orthopedic clinic follow-up with a repeat film is arranged.

note:
75-year-old male, new pt visit geriatrics clinic for wt loss and decline. Accompanied by daughter (primary caregiver), who provides part of Hx.
CC: wt loss ~12 lb over 4 mo per daughter. Pt says 'maybe a few pounds.' Chart wt 166 lb 6 mo ago, today 154 lb (clinic scale).
Poor appetite, eats about half of each meal, skips breakfast. Daughter notes he is more withdrawn and stopped cooking since his wife died 8 mo ago. Pt c/o fatigue and mild early satiety. Denies dysphagia, abd pain, N/V, diarrhea, melena, hematochezia, cough, night sweats, fever.
Daughter reports 2 near-falls when rising from a chair; pt denies any falls. Dentures ill-fitting x months w/ chewing difficulty.
PMH: HTN, T2DM, hyperlipidemia.
Meds: metformin 500 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Daughter fills pillbox weekly, no missed doses.
Vitals: BP 126/72 sitting, 118/68 standing, HR 70, Temp 36.6 C, SpO2 96% RA. BMI 21.4.
Exam: thin, temporal wasting, ill-fitting dentures, oral mucosa moist w/o lesions, lungs clear, abd soft NT w/o mass, no LAD. Slow gait, TUG 16 sec, gait speed 0.6 m/s, reduced grip strength.
Screens: MoCA 23/30, GDS-15 score 6.
Data from last wk: albumin 3.2 g/dL, A1c 6.4%, TSH 2.1, Hgb 12.4, Cr 1.1; CXR no acute findings.
Impression: frailty w/ unintentional weight loss, likely multifactorial: grief/low mood, poor dentition, reduced intake. A1c 6.4% w/ wt loss, metformin may be contributing to poor appetite.
Rec:
- Stop metformin (A1c at goal, anorexia)
- Start mirtazapine 7.5 mg qhs for appetite + mood
- Cont lisinopril, atorvastatin
- Dietitian referral, oral nutrition supplement BID between meals
- Dental referral for dentures
- PT referral for strength + balance
- SW referral: meals on wheels, grief counseling
- Labs: CMP, CBC, ferritin; FIT for colon ca screening
- Wt check + RTC in 4 wk

note:
This 72-year-old female returns for follow-up of polymyalgia rheumatica, diagnosed about four months ago and treated with a prednisone taper. Her symptoms had resolved on prednisone 15 mg daily, but when she reduced the dose to 7.5 mg daily two weeks ago her morning stiffness in the shoulders and hips returned, and it now lasts about 90 minutes. She has trouble raising her arms to comb her hair and getting out of a low chair, and she also reports fatigue. She denies headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain with chewing, vision changes, fever, and weight loss, which makes giant cell arteritis unlikely. She has hypertension controlled on amlodipine 5 mg daily, and a bone density scan last year showed osteopenia.

On exam her blood pressure is 136/80 and her heart rate is 72. The temporal arteries are non-tender with normal pulses. She has pain and limited active range of motion at both shoulders on abduction and tenderness over the hip girdle, but proximal strength is 5/5. There is no synovitis in the hands, wrists, or knees.

Labs from this week show an ESR of 38 mm/hr, a CRP of 14 mg/L, a hemoglobin of 11.8 g/dL, and normal creatinine and liver enzymes.

My assessment is a flare of polymyalgia rheumatica during the prednisone taper, with no features of giant cell arteritis. Because this is her first relapse and she is at risk for steroid toxicity given her osteopenia and hypertension, we discussed adding a steroid-sparing agent and she agreed.

For the plan, I am increasing prednisone back to 10 mg daily and will hold that dose for four weeks before restarting a slower taper of 1 mg every four weeks. She will start methotrexate 10 mg once weekly with folic acid 1 mg daily, and I counseled her that methotrexate is taken only one day a week, never daily, that she should limit alcohol, and that she should call for fever, cough, or mouth sores. I ordered hepatitis B and C serologies, a CBC, and a metabolic panel before the first dose, with monitoring labs repeated in four weeks. I am also starting alendronate 70 mg once weekly for bone protection during prolonged steroid use. She will continue amlodipine 5 mg daily. Follow-up in six weeks.
summary: A 72-year-old female with polymyalgia rheumatica on a prednisone taper returned with recurrent morning stiffness of the shoulders and hips after reducing to 7.5 mg daily, and she also reports fatigue. She denies headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain, vision changes, fever and weight loss. ESR is 38 mm/hr and CRP is 14 mg/L, and there is no synovitis or temporal artery tenderness. The assessment is a polymyalgia rheumatica flare without features of giant cell arteritis. Prednisone is increased to 10 mg daily, methotrexate 10 mg once weekly with folic acid and alendronate 70 mg once weekly are started, baseline labs are ordered, and follow-up is in six weeks.

Start methotrexate 10 mg once weekly with folic acid 1 mg daily; counseled on weekly-only dosing, limiting alcohol and calling for fever, cough or mouth sores
Order hepatitis B and C serologies, CBC and metabolic panel before the first dose, with monitoring labs in four weeks
Start alendronate 70 mg once weekly for bone protection
Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily
Follow-up in six weeks

note:
This 35-year-old male was referred to gastroenterology for iron-deficiency anemia found on routine blood work by his primary care doctor. He has limited health literacy, so I used plain language, asked him to repeat the plan back to me in his own words, and gave him a picture-based instruction sheet. He told me he cannot read the lab results on the patient portal.

He says he has felt tired for about six months and gets dizzy when he stands up fast. He craves ice and chews a cup of it every day. He denies black or tarry stools, blood in the stool, belly pain, vomiting blood, weight loss, trouble swallowing, and changes in his bowel habits. He eats meat a few times a week. He has had back pain from his warehouse job for a year and takes ibuprofen 600 mg about three times a day for it. He drinks alcohol rarely and does not smoke. He has no known family history of colon cancer or celiac disease.

Vitals today are BP 118/72 and HR 84, with a BMI of 24. He has mild conjunctival pallor. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with no masses or enlarged liver or spleen. A rectal exam showed brown stool that was negative for blood.

Labs from last month show a hemoglobin of 10.4 g/dL, an MCV of 72, a ferritin of 8 ng/mL, and normal kidney function.

My impression is iron-deficiency anemia in an adult male, which is concerning for slow blood loss from the gut. His frequent ibuprofen use may be causing stomach or duodenal ulcers or gastritis, and celiac disease is also possible, so he needs a full evaluation of both the upper and lower gut.

Plan: stop the ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for back pain instead. Start pantoprazole 40 mg daily before breakfast. Start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once every other day, taken with orange juice and not with milk or tea. Schedule an upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsies and a colonoscopy. The nurse reviewed the bowel prep with him using a pictorial sheet, and a nurse navigator will call him to go over it again. Order tTG-IgA, total IgA, and an H. pylori stool antigen. Repeat the CBC and ferritin in 8 weeks. He should go to the emergency room for black stools, vomiting blood, or fainting, and he correctly repeated these warning signs back to me.
summary: A 35-year-old male with limited health literacy was referred for iron-deficiency anemia with six months of tiredness, dizziness on standing and ice craving. Doctor: Good afternoon. I understand you're a 45-year-old female coming in about hot flashes. Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: For about eight months now I get these waves of heat in my face and chest, maybe six or seven times a day, and I wake up at night with night sweats. My periods have also become irregular.
Doctor: I see you were in the hospital about three weeks ago. What happened?
Patient: I had pneumonia and stayed four days. They gave me antibiotics and I'm all better now.
Doctor: Good. Any fever, cough, or chills now? Night sweats can worry me a bit after an infection.
Patient: No fever, no cough, no chills. The sweats started way before I got sick.
Doctor: Any chest pain, leg swelling, or history of blood clots?
Patient: No, none of that.
Doctor: Your blood pressure today is 120 over 76 and your heart rate is 72. Your lungs sound clear. The thyroid test they did in the hospital was normal, too. All of this fits with perimenopause.
Patient: Okay. Is there something I can take? The hot flashes are really bothering me and I can't sleep.
Doctor: Yes. I'd like to start an estradiol patch, 0.05 mg a day, changed twice a week, and also micronized progesterone 100 mg at bedtime to protect your uterus. We'll check in again in three months. If you get leg swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath, call us right away.
Patient: That sounds good. Thank you.

The impression is perimenopause. An estradiol patch and micronized progesterone at bedtime are started, with a recheck in three months.

This 45-year-old female is seen in cardiology clinic for resistant hypertension. Her blood pressure has stayed above goal for the past year despite taking a single-pill combination of amlodipine-valsartan-hydrochlorothiazide 10/320/25 mg once daily, which is at full doses. Her home log averages 152/94. She confirms that she takes the pill every day, her pharmacy records show on-time refills, and she does not use NSAIDs, decongestants, or herbal supplements and drinks very little alcohol. She denies headache, chest pain, palpitations, vision changes, and leg swelling. She mentions loud snoring, though no one has seen her stop breathing in sleep.

Office blood pressure is 156/96 in the right arm and 154/96 in the left arm, with a heart rate of 76. Heart sounds are normal with no murmur, the lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema. Labs from last week show a potassium of 3.3 mmol/L despite a normal creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL, and an aldosterone of 24 ng/dL with a suppressed renin, giving an elevated aldosterone to renin ratio even though she takes an ARB, which would be expected to hide it.

My impression is resistant hypertension with likely primary aldosteronism.

The plan is to add spironolactone 25 mg daily to her current pill, recheck potassium and creatinine in one week, and refer her for an adrenal CT scan and an endocrinology evaluation. I will also order a home sleep study because of the snoring. She will keep her home blood pressure log and bring it to follow-up in four weeks. She was advised not to take potassium supplements or salt substitutes once spironolactone is started.

note:
This 43-year-old female is seen in cardiology clinic for peripheral artery disease with claudication. Over the last eight months she has developed cramping pain in the left calf after walking about one block, which goes away within a few minutes of standing still, and the right calf has now started to cramp at about two blocks. She denies pain at rest, foot ulcers, color change in the toes, chest pain, and shortness of breath. She smokes about one pack per day and has a 25 pack-year history. She also has type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia. Her medications are metformin 1000 mg twice daily and pravastatin 20 mg daily, and she is not taking an antiplatelet drug. She has no history of heart failure and had a tubal ligation several years ago.

She lives alone in a third-floor apartment without an elevator, has no family nearby, and does not own a car, so she depends on the bus to reach appointments and the pharmacy. She says that no one is available to help with rides or to check her feet, and she has missed two prior clinic visits because she could not get transportation.

Today her BP is 142/86 and her HR is 82, with a BMI of 31. Femoral pulses are 2+ bilaterally, but the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent on the left and faint on the right. The left foot is cooler than the right with mild hair loss, capillary refill is 3 seconds, and there are no ulcers or gangrene. The ankle-brachial index is 0.62 on the left and 0.78 on the right. Her LDL is 138 mg/dL, her hemoglobin A1c is 7.8%, and her creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL.

My impression is symptomatic peripheral artery disease with lifestyle-limiting claudication, driven by active smoking, an LDL above goal, and diabetes.

Plan: start aspirin 81 mg daily. Stop pravastatin and start atorvastatin 80 mg daily. Start cilostazol 100 mg twice daily, 30 minutes before breakfast and dinner, since she has no heart failure. Continue metformin. I counseled her on smoking cessation for ten minutes and placed a quitline referral. Because she lives alone and cannot easily get to a supervised exercise program, I recommended a home walking program of 30 minutes three times a week, walking until moderate calf discomfort. I referred her to social work for help with transportation and to podiatry, and she will inspect her feet daily with a mirror. A clinic nurse will call her in two weeks to check on her progress, since she has no one at home to check in on her. She was given a written list of warning signs, including rest pain, a foot wound, or a cold or blue foot, and told to call the clinic or 911. Order an arterial duplex of the lower extremities. Follow-up in six weeks.

Left pedal pulses are absent and the ankle-brachial index is 0.62 on the left and 0.78 on the right, with LDL 138 mg/dL and A1c 7.8%. note:
This 22-year-old female presents to the infectious disease clinic with early Lyme disease after only partly completing her antibiotic. About two weeks ago she found an engorged tick on her left thigh after hiking in the woods, and ten days ago she noticed a red, expanding rash at that site. She was seen at an urgent care center eight days ago, diagnosed with erythema migrans, and prescribed doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days. At the pharmacy she could only afford to buy 8 tablets because she has no prescription coverage, so she took the doxycycline for four days and then ran out. She did not tell anyone because she was embarrassed. The rash has continued to enlarge since she stopped.

She reports fatigue, a mild headache, and aching muscles. She denies neck stiffness, facial drooping, palpitations, lightheadedness, chest pain, joint swelling, and fever. She takes acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for the headache. She has no known drug allergies. A urine pregnancy test done today was negative.

Vitals today are temperature 37.6 Celsius, BP 112/70, and heart rate 80. On exam she is well appearing. There is a 9 cm annular erythematous patch with central clearing on the left thigh, with no vesicles and no other skin lesions. She has no facial palsy, her neck is supple, her heart rhythm is regular without a murmur, and there are no joint effusions. An ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with a PR interval of 160 ms and no AV block.

My impression is early localized Lyme disease with erythema migrans, partially treated because of cost-related nonadherence, with no signs of carditis or neurologic involvement. Serologic testing is not needed because erythema migrans is a clinical diagnosis.

The plan is to restart doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for a full 14 days from today. To address the cost problem, the clinic pharmacy will dispense the entire supply today at no charge, and a social worker will review her eligibility for prescription assistance. I counseled her to take the tablets with a full glass of water and food, to stay upright for 30 minutes afterward, and to use sun protection. She will continue acetaminophen as needed. She will get a phone call in one week and return to clinic in two to three weeks, sooner if she develops facial weakness, palpitations, severe headache, or neck stiffness.

She reports fatigue, a mild headache and aching muscles, and denies neck stiffness, facial drooping, palpitations and fever. Exam shows a 9 cm annular patch on the left thigh and a normal ECG. The impression is early localized Lyme disease, partially treated because of cost, without carditis or neurologic involvement. Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily is restarted for 14 days, supplied free by the clinic pharmacy, with follow-up in two to three weeks.
